scenes.text: Plug in your phone at three in the morning. Then plug it into the same outlet at three in the afternoon. Same wall, same wires, same meter.

But depending on where you live, the power plants on the other end of that wire can be completely different. At night, a wind farm a few hundred miles away. In the afternoon, a field of solar panels that was dark twelve hours earlier.
So here's the idea for this video. The grid isn't one machine. It's a different machine every hour, rebuilt over and over, all day long, while you sleep and while you work.

We'll follow one day, hour by hour. By the end, you'll know why the hardest hour for the grid usually isn't the hottest one. And why, some days, power plants actually pay to give their electricity away.
scenes.graphic: 24-hour clock dial: 3 a.m. and 3 p.m. marked, icons for wind, nuclear, solar, battery, gas

scenes.text: Let's start in the dark. According to the Energy Information Administration, U.S. electricity use typically bottoms out around five in the morning. Most people are asleep, and most offices are closed.
scenes.graphic: line chart: typical U.S. hourly electricity demand over 24 hours, low point near 5 a.m.

scenes.text: But it never drops to zero. Refrigerators, pumps, servers and street lights keep running. That steady floor of demand is what the industry calls baseload.
The classic baseload plant is nuclear. A reactor costs a lot to build but very little to run, so operators keep it at full power around the clock.

In 2025, the average U.S. nuclear plant ran at 91 percent of its maximum possible output, higher than any other kind of power plant, according to the EIA. Nuclear supplied about 18 percent of the country's utility-scale electricity that year.
scenes.graphic: flat line chart: nuclear output across 24 hours vs. curved demand line

scenes.text: Now add the wind. In the middle of the country, the EIA says land-based wind is usually strongest overnight. So wind records there tend to fall in the early morning hours.
Take the Southwest Power Pool, the grid operator for a big stretch of the Great Plains. On April 27, 2020, between one and two in the morning, wind supplied 72 percent of its electricity demand.
scenes.graphic: map: Southwest Power Pool footprint with wind farms; callout '72% wind, 1-2 a.m., April 27, 2020'

scenes.text: By 2023, wind made up 36 percent of everything that grid generated across the whole year. Some nights there's more wind than anyone needs, and operators actually turn turbines down in the early morning to keep supply matched to demand.
Twelve hours later, the machine looks completely different. The sun is high, air conditioners are running, and in a growing number of places, solar is doing the heavy lifting.
Texas is a good example. In the summer of 2025, solar plants on the main Texas grid averaged 24 gigawatts between noon and one p.m. Two summers earlier, it was 12. That's double in two years.
scenes.graphic: bar chart: ERCOT average solar output at noon, summer 2023 (12 GW) vs. summer 2025 (24 GW)

scenes.text: And natural gas made room for it. Gas supplied half of the Texas grid's midday power in the summer of 2023, and 37 percent in the summer of 2025.
California went even further. In 2024, solar met almost half of the California grid operator's demand between eight in the morning and four in the afternoon.
And in the first five months of 2026, utility-scale solar generated more electricity than natural gas on 82 percent of days on that grid, up from 21 percent in 2024 and 2025.
So at 3 a.m. in Kansas you might be running on wind and nuclear, and at 3 p.m. in California mostly on sunshine. Same country, same kind of outlet, a different machine.
Now here's the twist I promised. You'd think the hardest moment for the grid is the hottest afternoon. Often it isn't. It's the hour right after the sun starts going down.
To see why, grid operators look at something called net load. That's total demand minus whatever wind and solar are producing. It's the part every other power plant has to cover.
scenes.graphic: diagram: total demand minus wind and solar equals net load, stacked area illustration

scenes.text: Plot net load over a typical spring day in California and it sags deep in the middle, then shoots up steeply in the evening. It looks like the outline of a duck, so that's what everyone calls it: the duck curve.
scenes.graphic: line chart: CAISO net load on a typical spring day, duck-shaped curve with belly at midday and steep neck at sunset

scenes.text: And the EIA says the duck's belly keeps getting deeper as more solar comes online.

The belly has its own problem. In spring, when it's mild and demand is low, there can be more solar than the grid can use. In 2024, California's grid operator curtailed 3.4 million megawatt-hours of wind and solar, 29 percent more than in 2023. Solar was 93 percent of it.
Then comes the neck. As solar fades around sunset, people get home, cook dinner and turn on lights and air conditioners. Everything that isn't the sun has to ramp up fast.
So keep that steep neck in mind. Because the most interesting part of this story is what's being built to fill it, and what it does to the price of electricity.

The fastest-growing answer is a battery. Charge it with cheap midday solar, then let it run in the evening. The EIA puts it neatly: storing midday solar flattens the duck's curve, and sending it out in the evening shortens the duck's neck.

The scale has changed fast. California's grid operator reported that in 2025, batteries in its market delivered about 9,100 megawatts on average in the hour ending at 8 p.m. In 2024, that figure was about 5,700.
scenes.graphic: line chart: average battery charging (midday, negative) and discharging (evening, positive) by hour, CAISO 2024 vs. 2025

scenes.text: Texas is following the same pattern. In the summer of 2025, batteries on its main grid supplied an average of 4 gigawatts in the 8 p.m. hour, right as the solar output was fading.
Batteries don't make energy, though. They shift it, and they lose some along the way. In 2019, the EIA found the U.S. battery fleet gave back about 82 percent of the electricity put into it.

And operators run them largely on price. In 2024, 41 percent of U.S. utility-scale battery capacity was used mainly for arbitrage. That's a fancy word for charging when power is cheap and selling it back when it's expensive.
Which brings us to price. On the wholesale market, where power plants sell to utilities, electricity can cost wildly different amounts from one hour to the next.
A Berkeley Lab analysis found the average U.S. wholesale price in 2023 was 36 dollars per megawatt-hour. But in California that year, hourly prices ranged from over 500 dollars down to below zero.
scenes.graphic: heat map: CAISO wholesale price by hour of day (x) and day of year (y), 2023, sunny spring hours in blue

scenes.text: Below zero. That's the open loop from the start. A negative price means sellers are paying buyers to take their power.

Why would anyone do that? The EIA explains that some plants can't easily or cheaply shut down for a short stretch. Nuclear operators try to run at full power. Big steam plants face costs every time they stop and restart.

And some wind and solar projects earn tax credits for every megawatt-hour they produce, so they may keep running even when the price dips below zero. For a few hours, paying a little beats shutting down.
In California's day-ahead market, prices were negative about 7 percent of the time in 2025, according to the grid operator's own market monitor. Most of those hours are sunny midday hours in spring.
scenes.graphic: bar chart: share of negative-price intervals in CAISO day-ahead market, 2024 (8.8%) vs. 2025 (7.1%)

scenes.text: On the other end are the expensive hours, when the grid calls on peaker plants. These are often gas turbines that run only a small slice of the year. They cost more to run, but they can start up quickly, which is exactly what that evening ramp needs.

Someone has to coordinate all of this, every second. That job belongs to balancing authorities. There are dozens of them across the country, and their job is to keep supply and demand matched in real time.

If supply and demand drift too far apart, the EIA warns, the result can be local or even wide-area blackouts. So operators forecast demand, line up plants ahead of time, trade power with neighbors, and adjust constantly.
scenes.graphic: diagram: balancing authority in the middle, arrows to generators, batteries, neighbor grids and customers

scenes.text: The best part? You can watch it yourself. The EIA's free Hourly Electric Grid Monitor shows demand, and the mix of sources by region, hour by hour. It's one of the best free tools on the internet if you want to see the machine change shape.
So what does any of this mean for you? Most of us never see those wholesale prices. But your timing still matters, and it matters more every year.

Most electric vehicle drivers charge overnight at home, according to the Department of Energy. And some utilities offer time-of-use rates, where electricity costs less in certain hours and more in others.
That only works because most homes now have meters that record use by the hour. In 2022, about 72 percent of U.S. electricity meters were smart meters, the EIA reports.

Here's the non-obvious part. The cheap hour on your grid might not be 3 a.m. anymore. In a sunny region it can be the middle of the day. So it's worth reading your own utility's rate plan instead of guessing.
Running the dishwasher or charging the car in a cheap hour isn't just about your bill. It's you helping the grid fill the duck's belly instead of its neck.
Quick recap. At 3 a.m., demand is near its low, nuclear runs flat out, and on the Great Plains, wind is often at its strongest.
At 3 p.m., solar takes over more and more of the load, sometimes so much that prices go negative. Then at sunset comes the steep neck of the duck, and batteries and gas plants race to cover it.
scenes.graphic: side-by-side stacked bars: example generation mix at 3 a.m. vs. 3 p.m. (illustrative, labeled by source)

scenes.text: The grid isn't one machine. It's a different machine every hour. And now you know how to read it.
Now I'm curious. What does your utility charge at night versus in the afternoon? Do you have a time-of-use rate, or one flat price? Tell me your state in the comments.

If you like seeing how the hidden machinery of everyday life really works, subscribe to The Hidden Grid. And if you want one short, sourced grid story in your inbox every week, check out our newsletter, The Grid Weekly.

meta.description:
At 3 a.m. and 3 p.m., the same outlet in your wall can be fed by completely different power plants.
We follow one day on the U.S. grid, hour by hour: wind and nuclear at night, solar at midday, and the steep evening ramp in between.

In this video:
- Why U.S. electricity demand bottoms out before dawn, and what baseload means
- Nuclear running flat out, and why Great Plains wind peaks overnight
- How solar took over the middle of the day in Texas and California
- Net load and the duck curve, explained simply
- Batteries shifting midday solar into the evening
- Why wholesale prices swing, and how they can go negative
- What balancing authorities do every second
- Why your timing (EV charging, time-of-use rates) matters
